description: This working paper develops a diagnostic framework for analyzing the limits of strategic reach through commitment overhang, strategic free capacity, and strategic optionality. It argues that great-power sustainability cannot be assessed through fiscal affordability or aggregate national power alone because strategic commitments draw on partially nonfungible resources and can impose different temporal burdens. The paper distinguishes high-burn commitments that consume current capability from lock-in commitments that encumber future capacity, and integrates protection recursion, regeneration bottlenecks, portfolio interaction, competitive expansion feedback, control-induced diversification, and justificatory portability. The 2026 U.S.–Israel–Iran conflict illustrates burn and restoration liabilities; Greenland illustrates prospective lock-in; and Canada–EU cooperation illustrates diversification intent. The paper concludes that strategic reach can continue to expand while discretionary capacity for future contingencies contracts, and that negative net conversion, declining free capacity, and loss of strategic optionality must be treated as distinct analytical outcomes.
abstract: Great-power overstretch is often framed as a mismatch between external commitments and economic resources. This paper develops a diagnostic framework centered on three linked concepts: commitment overhang, strategic free capacity, and strategic optionality. It integrates partially nonfungible resource bottlenecks, burn and lock-in portfolio effects, and external feedback. Additional strategic reach generates usable power only when cumulative converted value exceeds lifecycle and systemic burden and when sustainment and regeneration preserve minimum reserves. The 2026 U.S.–Israel–Iran conflict illustrates high-burn depletion; Greenland illustrates potential lock-in while distinguishing existing Pituffik obligations and pre-existing modernization from uncertain incremental commitments; and Canada–EU cooperation illustrates diversification intent without presuming measurable U.S. leverage loss. The paper uses the strategic poison pill only as a diagnostic metaphor for negative cumulative net conversion, distinct from optionality loss. The paper neither estimates a universal threshold nor claims that any case has crossed one. Its contribution is to integrate commitment portfolios, capacity regeneration, and external adaptation into a framework for explaining how strategic reach can expand while discretionary capacity for future contingencies contracts.

methodology.framework_name: Commitment Overhang–Strategic Free Capacity–Strategic Optionality Framework
methodology.research_design: Theory-building working paper using three contemporary developments as mechanism-based illustrations rather than matched cases for causal identification.
case_contexts: The 2026 U.S.–Israel–Iran conflict as a high-burn illustration of operational consumption, inventory depletion, and regeneration burden.
Greenland as a prospective high-lock-in illustration separating existing Pituffik obligations, pre-existing modernization, and uncertain incremental commitments.
Canada–EU cooperation as an illustration of diversification intent and institutional network-building under asymmetric dependence.
methodology.evidentiary_scope: The paper distinguishes directional mechanism evidence from prospective illustration and untested hypotheses. Public data do not place all capacity-stock variables on comparable units, so no universal threshold or quantified crossing is claimed.
methodology.core_problem: Whether accumulated commitments reduce residual discretionary capacity and strategic choice faster than regeneration, substitution, burden sharing, and adaptation can restore them.

analytical_lenses.name: Commitment Overhang

analytical_lenses.name: Strategic Free Capacity
analytical_lenses.description: Residual usable capacity after encumbrance and minimum reserve requirements.

analytical_lenses.name: Strategic Optionality
analytical_lenses.description: Decision space enabled by residual capacity under uncertainty.

analytical_lenses.name: Burn vs. Lock-In

propositions.title: Burn–Lock-In Proposition
propositions.statement: Strategic commitments impose different temporal burdens: burn commitments consume current capability, whereas lock-in commitments encumber future capacity.

propositions.title: Portfolio Interaction Proposition
propositions.statement: The combined burden of multiple commitments can exceed their individually assessed burdens because they compete for common inventories, logistics, industrial capacity, personnel, maintenance systems, political attention, and reserves.

propositions.title: Regeneration-Gap Proposition
propositions.statement: Strategic overstretch becomes more likely when, in at least one critical and weakly substitutable dimension, depletion plus net new commitments and reserve requirements persistently exceed usable regeneration.

propositions.title: Optionality Proposition
propositions.statement: An early manifestation of overstretch is a declining ability to address an additional contingency without weakening an existing obligation or breaching minimum reserves.

propositions.title: Justificatory Portability Hypothesis
propositions.statement: Security rationales used to justify expanded external control may become politically portable to competitors, but legitimation would require observable audience uptake or acceptance.

propositions.title: Control-Induced Diversification Proposition
propositions.statement: Repeated use of asymmetric dependence as coercive leverage can increase incentives for highly integrated partners to diversify, with effects depending on scale, switching costs, interoperability, and burden-sharing outcomes.

formulas.title: Cumulative Net Converted Value
formulas.description: Cumulative converted strategic value net of lifecycle and systemic burden over the observation or planning horizon.

formulas.title: Strategic Free Capacity
formulas.description: Residual usable capacity after existing encumbrance and minimum contingency reserves.

formulas.title: Capacity-Stock Transition
formulas.description: Usable stock transition for critical stock-like capacity dimension j.

formulas.title: Change in Strategic Free Capacity
formulas.description: Change in residual free capacity after regeneration, depletion, encumbrance, and reserve changes.

formulas.title: Net Capacity Pressure
formulas.description: Nonnegative pressure from depletion and net increases in commitment or reserve requirements.

formulas.title: Bottleneck-Pressure Ratio
formulas.description: Auxiliary diagnostic ratio comparing net pressure with usable regeneration in critical dimensions.

formulas.title: Marginal Net Conversion
formulas.description: Marginal difference between converted strategic value and lifecycle/systemic burden from an additional increment of strategic reach. Numbered (6) in the PDF.

formulas.title: Candidate Power Conversion Frontier
formulas.description: Candidate local crossing where marginal net conversion changes from positive to negative.

key_findings: Strategic sustainability can deteriorate before fiscal insolvency when depletion and new commitments reduce free capacity in a binding dimension faster than it can be restored.
Commitment overhang is a portfolio problem rather than a simple expenditure total.
Burn and lock-in commitments impose different temporal burdens and should be evaluated separately.
Protection recursion can cause lifecycle burden to exceed acquisition accounting.
Negative cumulative net conversion is distinct from loss of strategic optionality.
The 2026 U.S.–Iran operational dyad provides directional evidence of high-burn depletion and large restoration liabilities.
Greenland remains a prospective lock-in case because incremental obligations under the emerging security arrangement are not yet public.
Canada–EU cooperation demonstrates diversification intent and network-building but does not establish measurable U.S. leverage loss.
Control-induced diversification can either reduce exclusive leverage or improve burden sharing, so its net effect is ambiguous ex ante.
The decisive empirical signal of commitment overhang is forced trade-offs among reserves, programs, deployment cycles, and theater response capacity.
The Power Conversion Frontier is a conceptual threshold for empirical testing rather than a universal or already-estimated boundary.
policy_recommendations: Distinguish gross national capacity from residual strategic free capacity when assessing future commitments.
Separate present capability burn from future lock-in obligations in strategic portfolio analysis.

Track production lead times, replacement time, repair cycles, depot throughput, shipyard capacity, trained personnel, airlift and sealift utilization, and industrial expansion rather than relying on procurement dollars alone.
Separate existing obligations and pre-planned modernization from genuinely incremental commitments when assessing new agreements.
Treat partner diversification as a conditional network response whose effect depends on usable alternatives, switching costs, interoperability, and burden sharing.
Use forced trade-offs, reserve erosion, theater substitution, delayed programs, and extended deployment cycles as observable indicators of optionality pressure.
Do not infer threshold crossing from a single period, headline expenditure, or negative net-conversion result without dimension-specific and repeated evidence.
